summary.prose: s7 builds only the foundations the later cutover Stories need. Every subprocess a registered tool starts, in its approval preview, during the approval wait, in execute, in secondary commands and probes, and in the eight places where tools spawn processes themselves, goes through one process lifecycle: the executor resolves one effective signal for the call, and the lifecycle kills the whole process group and settles within 2 s when it aborts, so a client disconnect or the refresh's shared deadline stops the work, nothing is spawned after an abort, hooks run outside every tool's signal context, and an inventory test keeps new direct spawns out; each tool's own limit stays a ceiling and git_cat_file also takes a lowerable timeout; all 34 git tool definitions (plus four new ones) are listed in one typed list that drives registration and is checked for completeness by an inventory test, so callTool needs no cast; callTool refuses a registered tool that was not built from the definition passed, using a provenance table that only the failure-net wrappers write, and it accepts every exported gh tool and git definition; the gh tracker operations (fifteen, with every wrapper accounted for) are built on the op table through three additive internal argument variants and an additive string pattern on field specs, so owner and repo names are checked in the input schema before any approval, and the three paginated listings carry a fixed jq filter so every page is read as one line per item and returned in order; four git commands (config, ls-remote, update-ref, rm) are added with contracts taken from their real callers and every safety condition in the input schema; tools.call is a stream method that lets the terminal client run a tool with a validated caller; and a forbidden-spawn scan reports every direct git or gh spawn and direct builtin execute call. No call site moves here: s9 and s10 do that, and s10 turns the scan to failing mode.

hldContextSlice.frameworkSummary: Alternative a1: the executor in src/daemon/tools/executor.ts becomes the one pipeline for all external operations, and git, gh and Jira (acli) are registry tool families with an optional declared output schema and an approval class (none, common or destructive). Workflow and daemon code call tools through a typed helper that takes the tool definition; about 32 production files that spawn git or gh, or call a wrapper that does, move onto it in one change.

consumedContracts.name: Tool hook registry
consumedContracts.purpose: Lets a rule be registered against a tool id once and run after that tool succeeds for every caller, with failures reported on the result and not thrown.

consumedContracts.name: Tool output schema and typed call
consumedContracts.purpose: Lets a tool declare its result shape, has the executor check it when declared, and gives callers a result typed from the tool definition they pass.

consumedContracts.name: Approval class and approval exchange
consumedContracts.purpose: Defines the one field that gives a tool or call its approval class, the global setting that governs the common class, the request the executor sends to the attached client, the answer, the timeout and the denial reasons, so that every client implements the same exchange.

consumedContracts.name: CLI failure kinds
consumedContracts.purpose: One set of failure kinds returned by every git, gh and acli tool so callers tell a missing CLI, a missing sign-in, a time-out and a rejection apart.

boundary.internal: The repository check that fails on a direct git, gh or acli spawn outside src/daemon/tools, built first; the inventory it produces (about 32 production files known today, with the indexer, the design corpus reader, the analyze ignore filter, the understanding identity lookup and the daemon self-update included and no allowlist); the rewrite of every listed site and of the tests that import the old wrappers onto the typed helper; and the removal of runGit, commitAndPushArtifacts and the github.ts wrappers. It keeps the artifacts, commits and tracker records the same as before.

adjacentBoundaries.internal: The hook stage inside executeTool: the registry of hooks keyed by tool id, registration order, the rule that a hook runs only after a successful, checked call, and the way a hook failure is carried on the result. It places its stage at step 5 of the pipeline order in the architecture shape and does not own the schema check or the approval step.

The optional output-schema field and the check at step 4 of the pipeline, the typed call helper that takes a tool definition, the serial conversion queue, the key-value cross-check and the one-time escalation, and the shared failure kinds. It includes the choice of schema language and the way an input-to-tool mismatch is reported. It does not declare or read the approval class.

The approval step at step 2 of the pipeline: the single approval field on a tool definition, the global approval setting for the common class and its default, the IPC request and answer methods, the timeout value, the daemon-side holder of the pending requests, the terminal-client, editor and chat implementations of the answer, and removal of the 'auto-approving' fallback in executor.ts. It maps every existing requiresApproval flag, in every family, to the common class, and lists the tools that change. It does not choose which individual git, gh or Jira operations are destructive; each family Story marks its own.

The list of git operation families, their input and output schemas, which git operations are in the destructive class (for example force push, hard reset, clean, deleting a branch or tag), and the parsing of git porcelain output. Operations that need approval but cannot destroy work stay in the common class. Existing git ids keep their meaning.

The list of gh operation families, their schemas (read from gh --json where it exists, converted from text otherwise, for example gh pr diff and gh run view --log), which of the 27 gh operations that need approval are in the destructive class, and the 120 second time limit and its message. Existing gh ids keep their meaning.

The Jira tool families over acli (work item view, search, create, edit, transition, assign, comment, link, project list and view), their schemas, the --yes flag on every mutating command, the bounded forms of search and project list that acli requires, the 'acli jira auth status' sign-in check, and which operations are in the destructive class. An operation acli does not offer is left out and named as unsupported.
Private implementation of s8: Reach the rest of git through named, typed tools
Private implementation of s9: Move the workflow library's and the daemon's direct git and gh calls onto the registry
Private implementation of s10: Move the tracker and the terminal client onto the registry and remove the old paths

nonFunctional.performance: Each gh job has its own time limit from a table keyed by tool id and op, never shorter than the tool has today: reads 30 s (gh_pr_diff and gh_run_view 60 s, searches 60 s), changes 30 s by default, gh_issue_create 60 s, gh_pr_create 90 s, gh_pr_merge and gh_release_create 180 s, gh_repo_create and gh_repo_fork 120 s, downloads and uploads 300 s, gh_repo_clone 600 s, codespace create and rebuild 600 s (decided with the user on 2026-10-25; the daemon is expected to become multi-threaded so a slow gh will not block it). A timed-out call names the command and the limit, and a changing call adds that its outcome is unknown. The approval wait has its own timeout, set in s3's LLD. Conversion is serial, so a text-only tool that needs the cheap model costs one model call per attempt plus at most one escalated call; structured-output tools make no model call.
nonFunctional.security: No argument, setting, environment variable or caller identity can skip the approval for a destructive call; with no client attached the call is denied. Common calls follow one global setting. Approval requests travel only over the daemon's Unix socket. No credentials are read or stored: gh, git and acli use the user's own CLI sessions. A tool that declares an output schema and returns a result that does not match it fails and its result is not passed on. Today the executor runs every tool flagged requiresApproval as approved (11 git tools, 5 more by predicate, 27 gh operations and other families), so nothing asks; this Epic makes destructive calls ask every time and puts the rest under the global setting.
nonFunctional.observability: The executor logs each stage per call with the tool id, the caller, the approval class and decision and its reason, the schema check result, and each hook outcome. Hook failures, denials and conversion escalations are returned to the caller as part of the result, not only logged.
nonFunctional.durability: Pending approval requests are held in memory by the daemon and are lost on restart; a request left open at restart is treated as denied. Hooks are registered in code at start-up, not stored. The global approval setting is stored in the daemon's config. The cutover leaves artifacts, commits and tracker records unchanged.

dataModelChanges.details: Today deps.signal reaches only the approval broker, and a subprocess is cancellable only where a tool forwards the signal itself: ghExec accepts opts.signal but the legacy gh exports and its 'gh auth status' probe pass none, gitDiffTool passes none, and the approval preview of git_push and git_reset runs git before any ask. s7 adds src/daemon/tools/tool-signal.ts with a module-private node:async_hooks AsyncLocalStorage (already used in src/db/driver-work.ts), runWithToolSignal(signal, fn), runWithoutToolSignal(fn), currentToolSignal() and effectiveToolSignal(signal). executeTool resolves ONE effective signal first (deps.signal combined with the signal already in the context by AbortSignal.any, either alone, or undefined) and uses it for every cancellation check, for the preview (buildApprovalRequest runs inside runWithToolSignal(effective, ...), so the subprocesses an async buildApprovalGate starts are under the signal), for gate().ask(request, effective) (so the broker's cancellation listener exists for a nested gated call that has no signal of its own and the 300000 ms APPROVAL_WAIT_MS no longer outlives the outer call) and for tool.execute (inside runWithToolSignal(effective, ...)). PREVIEW BEHAVIOUR as it is: git_push without a ref calls readBranch (git symbolic-ref --short HEAD, 5000 ms) and git_reset calls currentBranch (the same command) and willNeedForcePush; when such a git command is killed they return { ok: false } or undefined and the builders return a preview object ('(unknown: <kind>)' for the ref, '(detached)' for the branch, a warning line for the force-push read). They do not throw, and buildApprovalRequest's generic-preview fallback applies only to a builder that throws. The call is stopped by the executor's cancellation check right after buildApprovalRequest returns, which returns the 'cancelled' denial before any ask. HOOKS: withHooks awaits runToolHooks on the continuation after execute, and an AsyncLocalStorage context follows continuations, so a nested executeTool entered from an outer tool's execute would run its hooks in the outer context (runWithToolSignal(undefined, fn) leaves a context unchanged). withHooks therefore runs runToolHooks inside runWithoutToolSignal, which runs the work with an explicit undefined store; inside a hook and every continuation of it currentToolSignal() is undefined, so a subprocess a hook starts is not cancelled by an unrelated outer call. With no signal anywhere nothing is stored and behaviour is as today. The context reaches every subprocess started on the async call chain, so no tool needs to forward the signal; the explicit deps.signal passing designed for the refresh tools stays as defence in depth. Scope of the guarantee, stated once: every SUBPROCESS of a registered tool (not of its hooks) is killed with its process group when the effective signal aborts and settles within 2 s; work that is not a subprocess (in-process HTTP, database or file operations) is not interrupted. Invariant it must not break: a call with no signal anywhere behaves as today; a tool that finishes normally is unaffected; hooks behave the same whoever called the tool.

dataModelChanges.entity: One process lifecycle with a streaming entry (spawnManaged) and the migration of the eight direct-spawn sites
dataModelChanges.details: Registered tools start processes in two ways today: through runShell and runShellBytes, and directly with node:child_process in five files, eight sites: builtins/shell/exec-detached.ts:116 (progress frames from stdout and stderr through deps.send, a maxRuntimeMs timer, 'bash -c' for the command form), builtins/k8s/index.ts:496, :641 and :769, builtins/test/index.ts:442, builtins/ssh/index.ts:237 and :503, and builtins/cloud/aws/logs.ts:104 (follow mode). Each spawns without a process group and attaches its handlers to the live child right after spawn (exec-detached calls onUtf8Data(child.stdout, ...), onUtf8Data(child.stderr, ...), child.on('error') and child.on('close')), kills only the parent (SIGKILL or SIGTERM) from its own abort listener on deps.signal, runs its own timer, and settles on 'close' with no bound; none reads the ambient signal. runShell spawns without a group and settles on 'close'; runShellBytes spawns detached and kills the group but settles only on 'error' and 'close'. s7 puts ONE lifecycle in src/daemon/tools/shell-helper.ts: before spawn it tests the effective signal (options.signal combined with currentToolSignal()); on non-win32 it spawns detached into its own process group (win32 keeps the single-process kill); on abort and on the timeoutMs ceiling (and, for runShellBytes, stderr overflow) it kills the group; if 'close' has not fired within a bounded 2 s after the kill it destroys the stdout and stderr streams, settles with what was captured and the aborted, timedOut or stderrOverflow flag, and clears its timers and listeners; a call that is not killed settles on 'close' as today. runShell and runShellBytes use it, and the new spawnManaged(cmd, args, options) exposes it for streaming tools. Its return is a DISCRIMINATED UNION: { spawned: true, child, settled } when a process was started, and { spawned: false, settled } when the effective signal was already aborted (settled is already resolved with aborted true). The eight direct-spawn sites are migrated to spawnManaged: each first checks 'spawned'; when it is false the site returns the aborted result it builds today for an abort and never reads child; when it is true the site attaches its handlers to the child exactly as before, passes its own limit as timeoutMs (exec-detached passes maxRuntimeMs), and drops its own kill timer and abort listener. A time-out or an abort now kills the group, and the result a site builds for a time-out or an abort keeps its current wording. shell:exec-detached with a command form ('bash -c') therefore ends its children too. An inventory test (child-process-inventory.test.ts) lists every .ts file under src/daemon/tools other than tests and fails when any file except shell-helper.ts imports node:child_process, so a new direct spawn cannot appear unnoticed. Invariant it must not break: a call that is not aborted or timed out produces the same output, progress frames and exit handling as today for each of the eight sites.

dataModelChanges.entity: Shared refresh deadline signal (how the budget reaches every tool)
dataModelChanges.details: The remaining time of the team policy refresh is carried by ONE AbortSignal, not by a per-call number. The caller (s9: src/workflow/team/policy-refresh.ts and src/workflow/team/git-async.ts, which today share one 10 s deadline and pass deadline.remainingMs() or 'timeout: left' to each call) creates the signal once at the start of the refresh from REFRESH_DEADLINE_MS (combined with its own abort) and passes it as deps.signal to every tool call it makes: git_fetch, git_fetch_refs, git_rev_parse, git_symbolic_ref, git_show, git_ls_tree, git_cat_file, git_ls_remote and git_config. Because every call watches the same signal, what is left shrinks by construction; a running command, and its whole process tree, is killed when it fires (through the explicit signal and the ambient context), the call settles within 2 s, and no later call starts (the executor and the lifecycle check it before starting). Each tool's own fixed limit stays a CEILING: the call stops at whichever comes first. git_cat_file additionally takes the lowerable timeoutMs for a caller that wants a shorter limit on one read. REFRESH_DEADLINE_MS stays 10 s and the lock-lifetime reasoning beside it is unchanged. s7 builds the receiving side and proves it with a test; s9 builds the sending side.

callTool (src/daemon/tools/call-tool.ts) runs executeTool(tool.id, ...) and casts result.data to the passed definition's output type, while registerTool overwrites an id with a warning. docs/plans/tool-registry.md records that, before s7, callTool must check that the registered tool under tool.id is the definition passed. The two families register differently. GIT: each file exports a plain definition and git/index.ts registers register(withFailureNet(tool)), a spread copy of the exported object. GH: withGhFailureNet is applied at the declaration ('export const ghProjectListTool = withGhFailureNet({...})', and defineGhFamily returns withGhFailureNet(...)), so the exported object IS the registered object and is already the wrapped copy; the inner literal is never exported. A rule that compares only outputSchema references is too weak ('{ ...original, execute: other }' keeps the same outputSchema and would pass); a rule that compares the registered tool's recorded original with the passed object would refuse every gh export. s7 adds src/daemon/tools/provenance.ts with a module-private WeakMap from a wrapper copy to the object it was built from, written ONLY by markDefinition(copy, original), read by definitionOf(registered), and the pure function isDefinitionOf(registered, tool). withFailureNet and withGhFailureNet call markDefinition(copy, tool) with the object exactly as passed (the IMMEDIATE original). isDefinitionOf is true when registered === tool, or when walking registered, definitionOf(registered), definitionOf(definitionOf(registered)), ... (at most 8 steps, so a cycle ends) reaches tool. callTool calls getTool(tool.id); if that is undefined, or isDefinitionOf(registered, tool) is false, it returns a rejected failure that names the id and runs nothing. Results: a git definition (registered copy marked from it) passes in one step; a legacy gh export or a defineGhFamily result (the registered object is the exported object) passes at once; an object wrapped twice passes for either level; a tool registered with a plain registerTool(definition) passes; a replacement made by spreading ('{ ...original, execute: other }'), with or without changed schemas or approval, is an unmarked new object whose chain never reaches the passed object and is refused, and so is that replacement wrapped by a failure net. A property or symbol on the definition is deliberately not used as the marker because a spread copies enumerable own and symbol properties. The public signature of callTool and TypedTool does not change. Invariant it must not break: callTool(tool) still works for every tool registered by registerGitTools and registerGhTools, whether passed the git definition or the exported gh object.

Protocol. tools.call is a STREAM method, because an RpcHandler receives only (params, context) with no send and no wire request id, while a StreamHandler receives (params, send, signal, context) and the server aborts its signal when the client closes the stream socket. Request params: { toolId: string, input: object, repoPath: string, caller: 'agent' | 'daemon' | 'workflow', approvalMode?: 'manual' | 'edit-auto' | 'auto' }. The handler validates the params (a missing or wrong field, a caller outside the enum, a non-object input) and answers with one 'error' frame { code: 'invalid-params', message } and closes. Otherwise it builds ToolDeps: sessionId is the string 'tools-call:' followed by context.connectionIdentity (or 'tools-call' when the handler has no context), following the precedent of a fixed daemon-side sessionId such as 'code-review' in src/workflow/runners/build/changed-files.ts; TrustedRpcContext and TrustedConnectionSession are not changed, and the git and gh tools keep no per-session state. repoPath comes from the params, send is the stream's own, requestId is a daemon-side monotonic counter, signal is the stream signal, caller and approvalMode come from the validated params, and connectionExecution is taken only from the trusted context, never from params. It runs executeTool and sends exactly one 'done' frame { result: ToolResult } (ToolResult includes failure and hookFailures). An unknown tool id is that same single response: the 'done' frame carries a failed ToolResult of kind rejected; it is never an IPC error. Tool progress frames are whatever the tool sends through deps.send. Cancellation contract (true for every subprocess of every registered tool, through the effective call signal and the one process lifecycle): when the client closes the stream the server aborts the signal; a pending approval, including a nested call's, resolves 'cancelled'; a tool not yet started does not start; every subprocess started in the approval preview or in execute, by a tool through the shell helpers or through spawnManaged, including secondary commands and probes, is killed with its process group and the call settles within the 2 s bound; nothing is spawned after the abort; work that is not a subprocess is not interrupted. Ownership: the call belongs to the stream that carries it; approvals are not tied to that connection: the daemon-wide broker pushes 'gate' frames to every client with an open approval.subscribe stream and answers arrive on approval.answer, so a client that wants approvals must hold an approval.subscribe stream; with none open a destructive call is denied no-client and a common call asks only under manual or edit-auto. Registered on the main thread in streamHandlers; worker threads have no registry. Change sites: src/daemon/handler-runtime.ts (streamHandlers entry), src/daemon/threads/method-class.ts (['tools.call', 'session', true]), src/shared/types.ts (ToolsCallParams and ToolsCallDone), a new src/daemon/tools/call-handler.ts, tests; src/daemon/server.ts, src/daemon/request-context.ts and src/shared/ipc-client.ts are unchanged because the generic stream path is used.

FieldSpec (src/daemon/tools/builtins/gh/op-table.ts) has kind, values, minimum, description and empty only, and fieldSchema's string branch returns Type.String with minLength 1 (unless empty) and the description, so an op field cannot carry a pattern. s7 adds an optional string property pattern to FieldSpec. fieldSchema's 'string' branch passes it to Type.String({ pattern, ...}) (the 'expr' branch ignores it). A helper field.name(description?) returns { kind: 'string', pattern: NAME_PATTERN } where NAME_PATTERN is the string '^(?!\\.{1,2}$)[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$' (an owner, repo, org or login; it refuses '.', '..', '/', '?', '#', '%', whitespace and non-ASCII). The pattern is a string, not a RegExp, because buildInputSchema compares a field two ops share with JSON.stringify of the spec minus description and values, which would hide a RegExp ({}) and now includes the pattern: two ops that give a shared field different patterns make defineGhFamily throw 'field x is declared differently by two ops'. A field in the flat input schema is Type.Optional unless every op requires it, so the pattern applies whenever the field is present. Because the executor checks the input schema before it builds the approval request, a bad owner, repo, org or login is a rejected input failure and never reaches an approval prompt; a refuse check inside execute would run after the approval step and is not used for this. Existing ops declare no pattern and build the schema they build today. Change sites: src/daemon/tools/builtins/gh/op-table.ts and its tests.

dataModelChanges.entity: Op-table argument variants path, kv and qs (internal, additive)
dataModelChanges.details: OpDef.command is a readonly string[] of fixed gh words and Arg has the variants pos, spread, last, flag and lit, so buildArgv cannot build one positional from several input fields, percent-encode a value, emit 'key=value' pairs or supply a constant query value; the gh_tracker ops need all of these. s7 adds three INTERNAL Arg variants to src/daemon/tools/builtins/gh/op-table.ts and teaches buildArgv about them; existing ops use none and are unchanged. (a) { path: readonly (string | { field: string })[] }: builds ONE positional from fixed text and field values, each field value passed through encodeURIComponent (so '/', '?', '#', '%' and Unicode cannot change the path), for example ['repos/', {field:'owner'}, '/', {field:'repo'}, '/issues/', {field:'number'}]. (b) { kv: string, flag: '-f' | '-F', field: string, repeat?: boolean }: emits the flag then 'key=<value>' (a list field with repeat true emits one flag-and-pair per member, the key being for example 'labels[]'); a field that is absent emits nothing. (c) { qs: readonly QsEntry[] } where QsEntry is one of { key: string, value: string } (a FIXED CONSTANT, emitted as given, never from input) or { key: string, field: string, optional?: boolean, join?: ',' } (a value from an input field: a string or integer is encodeURIComponent'ed; a list field requires join ',' and emits its members each encoded and joined by a literal ','). The qs variant is applied to the path positional that precedes it: entries are appended in the order declared as '?key=value&key=value'; an optional field entry that is absent is skipped; a required field entry that is absent is an input error caught by the op's required list before execute; when no entry remains nothing is appended (no bare '?'). A constant is the only way a fixed query value such as per_page=100 or state=all enters the argv, so there is no normalization or defaulting stage. GraphQL ops pass a FIXED query through lit (for example 'api','graphql','-f','query=<fixed text>') and the variables through kv. PAGINATION FRAMING: the existing lit variant carries a FIXED jq filter as the last two argv entries ('-q', '<filter>') of the three paginated ops; gh api --paginate prints one JSON array per page, which together are not one JSON document, so the filter makes gh print one JSON value per line across all pages, and the op's output builder reads stdout with parseJsonLines (blank lines skipped, an empty output is an empty list, a bad line is a rejected failure that names its line number). The filter is a constant of the op definition and never comes from input. owner and repo fields are field.name (see FieldSpec pattern) and number fields are positive integers, so no endpoint is ever an input and no value can alter the path. Outputs use the existing 'custom' out kind with a builder that parses the JSON (or the x-oauth-scopes header for token_scopes) into the declared shape. Exact argv produced (the fixtures; every one ends with the '-q' pair shown in the tracker family entity): comments_list with owner o, repo r, number 5: 'gh api --paginate repos/o/r/issues/5/comments?per_page=100 -q <comments filter>' and with since '2026-10-26T00:00:00Z' (colons encoded): 'repos/o/r/issues/5/comments?per_page=100&since=2026-10-26T00%3A00%3A00Z'; issues_by_labels with labels ['a','b c']: 'repos/o/r/issues?state=all&per_page=100&labels=a,b%20c'; issues_titles: 'repos/o/r/issues?state=all&per_page=100'. Change sites: src/daemon/tools/builtins/gh/op-table.ts, src/daemon/tools/builtins/gh/helpers.ts (parseJsonLines) and their tests.

One op-table family defined with defineGhFamily in a new file src/daemon/tools/builtins/gh/tracker.ts, using the FieldSpec pattern and the path, kv and qs variants, and REGISTERED by adding its import and registerTool(ghTrackerTool) to registerGhTools in src/daemon/tools/builtins/gh/index.ts (defineGhFamily does not register; its result is already the wrapped object, as for every other gh export). Every op declares input and output schemas; owner, repo, org and login are field.name fields; numbers are positive integers; the tool returns what the API returns and the wrapper-level transformations listed last stay for s10. PAGINATED OPS (4, 6 and 7 below) each carry --paginate and a FIXED constant jq filter through lit('-q', filter) placed after the path positional, so gh prints one JSON value per line across all pages, exactly as the existing wrappers in src/workflow/tracker/github.ts do (lines 284, 351 and 362); the builder reads the output with parseJsonLines, keeps API order, and a line that does not parse gives a rejected failure that names the line number. (5) comment_post: -X POST, path repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{number}/comments, kv -f body; {owner, repo, number, body}; {id}; common, 30 s; ghPostCommentReturningId (the existing gh_issue_comment returns no id). (13) user_by_host: a plain val('--hostname','host') flag, path users/{login}; {host, login}; {login, node_id}; none, 30 s; the lookup in src/understanding/identity.ts (the host and account loop stays in s9). It preserves the current behaviour: when the API gives no pageInfo the op returns pageInfo { hasNextPage: false } and omits endCursor; when the API gives hasNextPage false with a non-empty endCursor it returns both; issueCount is returned only when it is a number; the search-string building, the page-size clamp, the mapping of nodes to tasks and total stay in s10. MAPPED TO EXISTING OPS (closed table; no op is added later): ghCreateLabel to gh_label create with force; ghCreateIssue to gh_issue_create; ghGetIssueBody and ghGetIssueState to gh_issue_view with json fields body and state,labels; ghEditIssueBody and ghAttachMilestone to gh_issue_edit; ghComment to gh_issue_comment; ghCloseIssue to gh_issue_close; ghFindIssueByLabels(+Strict) and ghListRepoIssueUrls to gh_issue_list; ghFindProjectByTitle to gh_project_list with limit 200 (its data.projects rows carry number, title, url and closed, which is all the wrapper reads); ghAddProjectSingleSelectField to gh_project_manage field-create with dataType SINGLE_SELECT and singleSelectOptions (the wrapper reads only success); ghAddProjectItem to the legacy tool gh:project:item-add with url and owner (the wrapper reads only success). Raw gh api stays excluded from the gh coverage table, which gets a note that this family is s7's amendment (the user's decision of 2026-10-26).

dataModelChanges.entity: OpDef diagnostic field and the gh failure path
dataModelChanges.details: In ghFailureOf (src/daemon/tools/builtins/gh/helpers.ts) the spawn-error branch already returns original: o.stderr.trim(); for ordinary command-exit failures (missing-signin, unreachable, rejected) failure.original is set only from probe text, so an HTTP 422 text stays in failure.message; defineGhFamily forwards that failure before any output builder runs. The executor does NOT truncate a tool's own failure: executeTool returns a failed result from tool.execute unchanged ('if (!result.success) return result;'), and only the failed() helper it uses for its own failures slices failure.original to ORIGINAL_MAX_CHARS (4000). So the cap is applied by the seam itself. s7 adds an optional OpDef field (diagnostic: 'stderr') that defineGhFamily passes to ghFailureOf; when it is set, ghFailureOf puts the trimmed stderr (or, when stderr is empty, stdout) of a command-exit failure in failure.original, cut to FAILURE_ORIGINAL_MAX_CHARS, a constant defined once in gh/helpers.ts with the value 4000 and asserted equal to the executor's ORIGINAL_MAX_CHARS by a test. The spawn-error branch is unchanged. The cap and the text apply only to ops that opt in (issue_create_typed first); every other gh tool is unchanged, so no existing failure object changes. Change sites: src/daemon/tools/builtins/gh/op-table.ts and src/daemon/tools/builtins/gh/helpers.ts. Invariant it must not break: the failure objects of existing gh tools, including the spawn-error branch, shown by the s5 test files.

dataModelChanges.entity: git tools git_config, git_ls_remote, git_update_ref, git_rm (per-tool contracts)
dataModelChanges.details: Four typed git tools, each declared with satisfies TypedTool with concrete typebox input and output schemas (additionalProperties false), listed in gitToolDefinitions and so registered by registerGitTools as register(withFailureNet(tool)), passing deps.signal to runShell. EVERY SAFETY CONDITION LIVES IN THE INPUT SCHEMA: executeTool checks the input schema before it builds the approval request, while assertSafeArg runs inside execute after the approval step, so an unsafe value such as one containing a NUL reaches the destructive approval gate unless the schema refuses it. assertSafeArg stays as defence in depth. The schema patterns equal the callers' existing rules, so they refuse nothing a caller accepts today. SAFE_REF is exactly the predicate isSafeRefName (src/workflow/team/sighting-store.ts:60) written as one Unicode-aware pattern, not an ASCII class: it accepts any script, '+', '#' and other valid punctuation and rejects an empty name, a leading '-' or '/', whitespace and control characters (including NUL), the characters ~ ^ : ? * [ and backslash, '..', '@{', '//', the name '@', and a trailing '/', '.' or '.lock'. SAFE_PATH is only 'no NUL': a path may start with '-' because the argv puts '--' before the paths (assertSafeArg and handoff.ts do the same). An equivalence test runs the SAFE_REF pattern and isSafeRefName over one corpus. A missing, wrongly typed or unsafe field is a rejected input failure produced by the executor before any approval. cwd is optional everywhere and defaults to process.cwd() as in the other git tools. CONTRACTS. (1) git_config: input {cwd?, key} where key matches ^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9-]*(\\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]+)+$; argv ['git','config','--get',key]; output {found: boolean, value?: string}; exit 0 gives {found:true, value} with the trailing newline trimmed (an empty value is allowed); exit 1 with empty stdout is a SUCCESS {found:false} (identity.ts treats it as 'no email'); any other exit code, a cut output or a spawn error is a failure (kind from failureKind; identity.ts maps these to 'git identity unavailable'); ceiling 5000 ms; class none; callers: companion/header.ts reads user.name and understanding/identity.ts reads user.email. (2) git_ls_remote: input {cwd?, remote (SAFE_REF), heads?: boolean (default false), symref?: boolean (default false), patterns?: string[] (each SAFE_REF, default [], at most 8)}; argv ['git','ls-remote', '--symref' when symref, '--heads' when heads, remote, ...patterns]; output {entries: [{objectId, ref}], symrefs: [{ref, target}]} parsed from the output, where a line 'ref: refs/heads/main<TAB>HEAD' becomes the symref {ref:'HEAD', target:'refs/heads/main'} and a line '<sha><TAB><ref>' becomes an entry; an empty answer is a SUCCESS with empty lists (handoff.ts treats empty output as 'branch absent'); a non-zero exit is a failure classified with network true (an unreachable remote is 'unreachable'; git's text is in failure.message); ceiling 30000 ms; class none; callers: branch-resolution.ts uses symref true with patterns ['HEAD'] and heads true with patterns ['refs/heads/<name>']; handoff.ts uses heads true with patterns ['refs/heads/<branch>']. (3) git_update_ref: input {cwd?, ref (SAFE_REF and starting with 'refs/'), delete (the required constant true: only deletion is supported)}; argv ['git','update-ref','-d',ref]; output {ref, deleted: true}; git exits 0 when the ref is already absent, which is a success; any other exit is a failure with mutating set (a time-out says the outcome is unknown); ceiling 10000 ms; class destructive (always asks, but only for input that passed the schema); callers: team/handoff.ts deletes refs/heads/<tmpBranch> and a temporary ref. (4) git_rm: input {cwd?, paths: string[] (1 to 200 items, each SAFE_PATH), quiet?: boolean (default true)}; argv ['git','rm', '-q' when quiet, '--ignore-unmatch','--', ...paths]; output {paths: string[]} (the paths asked for); a path that matches nothing is a success because of --ignore-unmatch; any non-zero exit is a failure with mutating set; ceiling 30000 ms; class destructive (always asks, only after the schema); caller: team/handoff.ts runs it with cwd set to a worktree directory and one path. The s8 coverage table marks the four as built by s7 and s7's dependsOn stays s1 to s5. git_ls_remote and git_config are on the refresh's path and take the shared deadline signal like the other refresh tools.

dataModelChanges.entity: gitToolDefinitions: one typed list of all git definitions, with a mandatory inventory test
dataModelChanges.details: src/daemon/tools/builtins/git/index.ts imports the 34 definitions one by one and exports only registerGitTools, so no definition list exists for a fixture or a consumer to import. s7 adds src/daemon/tools/builtins/git/definitions.ts, which exports gitToolDefinitions: all git tool definitions (the 34 existing and git_config, git_ls_remote, git_update_ref and git_rm) as one list declared 'as const satisfies readonly TypedTool[]'. registerGitTools iterates this list and registers register(withFailureNet(tool)) for each (the existing tools keep their ids and their order), and src/daemon/tools/builtins/git/index.ts re-exports the list. The type fixture, the registration test and the s9 and s10 consumers import gitToolDefinitions directly. The satisfies clause checks only the elements that are IN the list; a definition declared in its own file and left out of the list still compiles, so the compiler does NOT guarantee that the list is complete and this design makes no such claim. Completeness is enforced by a mandatory inventory test (typed-git-tools.test.ts): it lists the .ts files of src/daemon/tools/builtins/git other than index, definitions, helpers, coverage and the tests, imports each, collects every export whose value has a string id and an execute function, and requires that set to equal gitToolDefinitions in both directions (a tool exported but not listed fails; a listed object not exported by a tool file fails), requires the ids to be unique, and requires the ids registered by registerGitTools to equal the ids of the list. The individual named exports (gitDiffTool and the rest) stay, and callTool(gitDiffTool, ...) passes the provenance check because the registered copy is marked as built from that exported object.

A script run in the build chain after tsc, beside scripts/check-model-definitions.mjs. It reads every non-test file under src outside src/daemon/tools with the TypeScript compiler and REPORTS each place that runs git, gh or acli (execFile, execFileSync, spawn, exec, runShell or runShellBytes with one of them first, a call into a wrapper module, an injected exec seam) and each direct call of a builtin tool's execute outside the executor (for example gitDiffTool.execute in src/workflow/code-review/grounding.ts and src/workflow/runners/build/changed-files.ts). It prints file and line and exits 0 in report mode; a flag switches it to failing mode, which s10 turns on. It carries one positive-control fixture per form. Exemptions written in the script with reasons: the daemon self-update (src/cli/services/maintenance.ts, src/daemon/installed-commit.ts) and src/indexer/index.ts only. It covers code outside src/daemon/tools; the child_process inventory test covers the inside.

dataModelChanges.entity: All 34 git tool definitions and the compile-time type check
dataModelChanges.details: There are 34 git tool files that export their definition as ': Tool', and every one declares a typebox outputSchema. s7 changes ALL 34 (a mechanical, declaration-only edit) to inferred objects checked with satisfies TypedTool, so Static<T['inputSchema']> and Static<T['outputSchema']> stay concrete for callTool; this covers gitDiffTool, which grounding.ts and changed-files.ts call directly today, and every tool the s9 and s10 replacement tables may name. registerGitTools wraps them with withFailureNet at registration, so the registered tool is a marked spread copy and the exported definition keeps its concrete type. Their runtime behaviour, ids and approval classes are unchanged (k7). The root tsconfig.json adds '**/__type-tests__/**' to its exclude list so the normal build neither compiles nor emits the fixtures. A dedicated tsconfig.typecheck.json extends it with noEmit true, an include of the fixtures under src/daemon/tools/__type-tests__ and an exclude that does not drop them, and an npm script typecheck:tools, added to the build chain after tsc. The fixture imports gitToolDefinitions and checks it against 'readonly TypedTool[]', and has positive and negative callTool fixtures (valid input, invalid input and a misspelt result field, using @ts-expect-error for the invalid ones) for gitDiffTool and the refresh tools. Invariant it must not break: today's behaviour of each tool, shown by the s4 and s5 test files that already run them.

interactionWithShared.howDetails: Hooks run inside executeTool for every caller, so a rule registered on a tool runs for a workflow call to it; they run through runWithoutToolSignal, outside every tool call's signal context (a nested call's hooks included), and only after a checked success. s7 registers no production hook; its tests register one and call the tool through callTool with caller 'workflow' and through tools.call.

The git tools keep concrete typebox schema types through satisfies TypedTool; the gh tracker family stays run-time checked per AMD-10. callTool gains the registered-definition provenance check the plan records for s7 (a side table written only by the two failure-net wrappers, walked from the registered tool to the passed object), with an unchanged signature, and TypedTool is unchanged.

A call follows shouldAsk: destructive always asks; common asks when the effective mode (deps.approvalMode, else tools.commonApproval, default auto) is manual or edit-auto. tools.call passes the validated caller and the optional approvalMode into ToolDeps; approvals travel over approval.subscribe and approval.answer as built by s3. git_update_ref and git_rm are destructive and always ask, and gh_tracker owner and repo names are pattern-checked, both only after the executor's existing input-schema check has passed. No approval rule is added and the pipeline order is unchanged; the executor resolves one effective signal, runs the preview and execute under it, passes it to the broker's ask so a pending approval of a nested call is cancelled, and returns denial 'cancelled', a value sc5 already defines. ToolDeps is not changed.

Failures use the existing kinds; an aborted call before execute is failed('denied') with denial 'cancelled'; a process stopped by the signal is a rejected failure that says it was cancelled, a limit that passes is timed-out, a callTool provenance refusal is a rejected failure, and a paginated tracker line that does not parse is a rejected failure naming the line; failure.original is an existing optional field, capped at 4000 characters by the gh diagnostic seam for the ops that opt in. No kind is added.

errorCases.scenario: The effective signal is already aborted, or is aborted while the approval preview is built, after the request is built and before the ask, or after the approval answer and before execute
errorCases.detection: executeTool resolves the effective signal first and tests it before buildApprovalRequest, after it returns, before gate().ask and immediately before tool.execute
errorCases.response: Returns failed('denied') with denial 'cancelled'; the tool is not started and no later approval answer is acted on
errorCases.userImpact: The stage that made the call fails with the cancellation reported

errorCases.scenario: A tools.call stream closes (or the shared refresh deadline fires) while the approval PREVIEW of git_push (no ref given) or git_reset is running git
errorCases.detection: buildApprovalRequest runs inside runWithToolSignal(effective, ...), so the preview's runShell calls (readBranch and currentBranch run 'git symbolic-ref --short HEAD', and willNeedForcePush runs its own git read) see the ambient signal and the lifecycle's abort listener fires
errorCases.response: The preview's process group is killed and settles within 2 s; the helper returns { ok: false } or undefined and the builder RETURNS a preview ('(unknown: <kind>)' for the ref in git_push, '(detached)' and a warning line in git_reset); it does not throw, so the generic preview is not used; the executor's cancellation check right after buildApprovalRequest returns the 'cancelled' denial before any ask
errorCases.userImpact: No preview subprocess outlives a cancelled call and no approval is requested for it

errorCases.scenario: A nested executeTool call to a destructive or common-under-manual tool has no signal of its own and is waiting for approval when the outer call is aborted
errorCases.detection: The executor resolves the effective signal as the signal already in the context combined with deps.signal and passes it to gate().ask(request, effective), so the broker installs its cancellation listener on it
errorCases.response: The pending approval resolves 'cancelled' at once instead of waiting for the 300000 ms approval timeout, and the nested call returns the cancelled denial
errorCases.userImpact: A nested call cannot outlive the outer call's cancellation while waiting for approval

errorCases.scenario: A nested executeTool, entered from inside an outer tool's execute, finishes its tool and runs its hooks while the outer call's signal is still live or aborts during the hook
errorCases.detection: withHooks runs runToolHooks through runWithoutToolSignal, which runs the hooks with an explicit undefined store; currentToolSignal() is undefined inside the hook and in every continuation of it, so the inherited outer context is not seen
errorCases.response: A subprocess the hook starts is not killed by the outer call's abort and runs under its own limits; the nested result still returns normally
errorCases.userImpact: A hook behaves the same whoever called the tool; an unrelated outer abort cannot cancel it

errorCases.scenario: A tools.call stream closes (or the shared refresh deadline fires) while a LEGACY tool that does not forward deps.signal is running: git_diff, a legacy gh export such as ghProjectListTool, or a multi-command tool
errorCases.detection: executeTool ran tool.execute inside runWithToolSignal, so currentToolSignal() is the effective signal; the shared lifecycle's abort listener on the effective signal fires for every subprocess the tool has running
errorCases.response: The lifecycle kills each subprocess's process group and settles within 2 s with the aborted flag; the tool returns the rejected failure its own error handling builds for an aborted command; no later subprocess of that tool starts because each one tests the effective signal before spawn
errorCases.userImpact: A disconnect or deadline stops the work instead of leaving processes running until their own limit (up to 600 s for gh_repo_clone)

errorCases.scenario: The stream closes while ghExec's ambiguous-error 'gh auth status' probe is running
errorCases.detection: The probe's runShellBytes call runs inside the same async call chain, so its effective signal includes the ambient tool signal even though the call passes no signal option
errorCases.response: The probe's process group is killed and its call settles within 2 s; ghExec treats a probe it could not complete as no probe text and the tool returns its failure
errorCases.userImpact: No sign-in probe outlives a cancelled call

errorCases.scenario: A tool that spawns its own process (shell:exec-detached including its 'bash -c' command form, a k8s tool, the test runner, an ssh tool, aws logs tail in follow mode) starts with an effective signal that is already aborted
errorCases.detection: spawnManaged returns the union branch { spawned: false, settled } because the effective signal is aborted on entry; the site checks 'spawned' before it reads child
errorCases.response: Nothing is spawned and no handler is attached; the site returns the aborted result it builds today for an abort, with no progress frames
errorCases.userImpact: No process starts after a deadline or a cancel and no site touches a missing child

errorCases.scenario: The stream closes while a tool that spawns its own process is running
errorCases.detection: The site was migrated to spawnManaged ({ spawned: true, child, settled }), whose effective signal is options.signal combined with currentToolSignal(); the abort listener fires
errorCases.response: The whole process group is killed (not only the parent), settled resolves within 2 s, the tool builds its usual aborted result, and progress frames stop; a descendant that holds the stdout or stderr pipe cannot keep the call open past the bound
errorCases.userImpact: A streaming tool stops with its children instead of leaving them running

errorCases.scenario: A tool that spawns its own process is time-limited by its own ceiling (maxRuntimeMs of exec-detached, a test or ssh time-out) and the ceiling passes
errorCases.detection: spawnManaged's timeoutMs timer fires and sets timedOut
errorCases.response: The process group is killed, settled resolves with timedOut true within 2 s, and the tool builds the time-out result it builds today
errorCases.userImpact: A time-out now ends the children too; the message is unchanged

errorCases.scenario: A new file under src/daemon/tools imports node:child_process
errorCases.detection: The inventory test (child-process-inventory.test.ts) lists every non-test .ts file under src/daemon/tools and finds an import of node:child_process outside shell-helper.ts
errorCases.response: The test fails and the build's test sweep fails
errorCases.userImpact: A tool cannot add a spawn that bypasses the lifecycle without being noticed

errorCases.scenario: runShell or runShellBytes is given an already-aborted effective signal (its own, or the ambient one)
errorCases.detection: The lifecycle tests the effective signal on entry, before spawn
errorCases.response: Returns without starting a process: code null, spawnError false, aborted true; the git helper fail() turns it into a rejected failure that says the call was cancelled and nothing ran
errorCases.userImpact: No command starts after a deadline or a cancel

errorCases.scenario: The shared refresh deadline signal fires while a refresh tool's command is running
errorCases.detection: The abort listener the lifecycle installed kills the child's process group; the result has code null and a kill signal, so ranToExit is false
errorCases.response: The tool returns a rejected failure naming the cancellation; a changing command adds that its outcome is unknown; later refresh calls fail at the executor check without starting
errorCases.userImpact: The refresh stops at the shared deadline and starts no call after it

errorCases.scenario: A command has started a descendant (a transport or helper process) that keeps the stdout or stderr pipe open after the parent is killed
errorCases.detection: The lifecycle kills the whole process group on abort, time-out and (runShellBytes) stderr overflow; if 'close' has not fired 2 s after the kill, its bounded-settlement timer fires
errorCases.response: The group kill removes the descendant; if a pipe is still open the lifecycle destroys the stdout and stderr streams and resolves anyway after 2 s with what was captured and the aborted, timedOut or stderrOverflow flag, and clears its timers and listeners
errorCases.userImpact: A call cannot outlive the deadline by more than the 2 s settlement bound, and no helper process is left running

errorCases.scenario: The shared deadline fires between two refresh calls
errorCases.detection: executeTool tests the effective signal before the next call's approval request and before execute
errorCases.response: The next call returns denied with cancelled and its command never starts
errorCases.userImpact: A refresh cannot run past its 10 s budget by starting another call

errorCases.scenario: The signal is aborted between the commands of git_show (header, diff, stat)
errorCases.detection: git_show tests deps.signal.aborted before each command, and each shell call tests the ambient signal on entry
errorCases.response: The commands after the abort do not start; the tool returns a rejected failure
errorCases.userImpact: A multi-command tool does not run past the deadline

errorCases.scenario: A registered tool does non-subprocess work (an in-process HTTP, database or file operation) when the signal aborts
errorCases.detection: No lifecycle is involved; the work is not a subprocess
errorCases.response: It is not interrupted and finishes or stops by its own means; this is outside the stated guarantee and is recorded as an open question
errorCases.userImpact: Cancellation is a guarantee about subprocesses, not about every kind of work

errorCases.scenario: callTool is given a definition whose id is not registered
errorCases.detection: getTool(tool.id) returns undefined
errorCases.response: A rejected failure that names the id; nothing is run
errorCases.userImpact: A typed caller cannot run a tool that is not in the registry

errorCases.scenario: callTool is given a definition whose id is registered to a replacement: another tool registered over the id, including a spread copy of the definition with a different execute, inputSchema, outputSchema or approval that keeps the same outputSchema object, or such a copy wrapped by a failure net
errorCases.detection: callTool evaluates isDefinitionOf(registered, tool): registered is not the passed object, and the chain registered, definitionOf(registered), ... (provenance WeakMap written only by markDefinition in the two failure-net wrappers) never reaches it within 8 steps, because a replacement made by spreading is an unmarked new object and a wrapper around it is marked from the replacement, not from the passed object
errorCases.response: A rejected failure that names the id; nothing is run and no data is returned under the wrong type
errorCases.userImpact: A typed caller cannot receive data produced by a different implementation than the definition it passed

errorCases.scenario: callTool is given a git definition whose registered tool is its withFailureNet copy
errorCases.detection: git/index.ts registers register(withFailureNet(tool)); the wrapper called markDefinition(copy, tool), so definitionOf(registered) is the passed object
errorCases.response: The provenance check passes after one step and the call runs
errorCases.userImpact: None: every registered git tool stays callable

errorCases.scenario: callTool is given an exported gh tool or family (a legacy export such as ghProjectListTool, or the defineGhFamily result including gh_tracker)
errorCases.detection: The export is already the object returned by withGhFailureNet and registerGhTools registers it as it is, so registered === tool; its recorded original (the inner literal) is not needed and is not compared
errorCases.response: The provenance check passes at once and the call runs
errorCases.userImpact: None: every exported gh tool stays callable

errorCases.scenario: callTool is given a definition that was wrapped twice, passing either level
errorCases.detection: markDefinition records the immediate original at each wrapper, so the walk from the registered object reaches both the inner and the outer object
errorCases.response: The provenance check passes for either object
errorCases.userImpact: None

errorCases.scenario: A git tool is exported from its file but missing from gitToolDefinitions, or a listed object is not exported by a tool file
errorCases.detection: The inventory test (typed-git-tools.test.ts) imports every git tool module, collects every export that has a string id and an execute function, and compares that set with gitToolDefinitions in both directions; the compiler cannot detect the omission because 'satisfies readonly TypedTool[]' checks only listed elements
errorCases.response: The test fails and the build's test sweep fails; registerGitTools would otherwise leave the tool unregistered
errorCases.userImpact: A tool that exists in code but not in the list, the registry or the type check is caught before release

errorCases.scenario: git_config reads a key that is not set
errorCases.detection: git config --get exits 1 with empty stdout
errorCases.response: Success with {found: false}; no failure
errorCases.userImpact: The caller (identity lookup, header) treats it as 'no value' exactly as it does today

errorCases.scenario: git_config fails for another reason (exit other than 0 or 1, cut output, spawn error, bad config file)
errorCases.detection: The exit code, ShellResult.stdoutTruncated or ShellResult.spawnError
errorCases.response: A failure whose kind comes from failureKind (missing-tool for a spawn error, rejected otherwise)
errorCases.userImpact: The identity lookup reports 'git identity unavailable'; the header omits the name

errorCases.scenario: A new git tool gets an unsafe value: a key that is not dotted, a ref (or remote, or pattern) that isSafeRefName refuses (leading '-' or '/', whitespace, control characters, ~ ^ : ? * [ backslash, '..', '@{', '//', '@', trailing '/', '.' or '.lock'), a ref outside refs/, a path with a NUL, delete other than true, empty or oversized paths, more than 8 patterns
errorCases.detection: The tool's input SCHEMA (patterns, const, minItems, maxItems), which executeTool checks before it builds the approval request
errorCases.response: A rejected input failure produced by the executor; the approval gate is not called and nothing runs, whether or not an approval subscriber is attached
errorCases.userImpact: Unsafe input never reaches an approval prompt and the destructive tools only ever ask about input that already passed

errorCases.scenario: A branch or remote name that the real callers accept (Unicode, '+', '#') is given to a new git tool
errorCases.detection: SAFE_REF is the isSafeRefName predicate as one Unicode-aware pattern, so the schema accepts exactly what the callers accept
errorCases.response: The call proceeds as it does through the old direct git call
errorCases.userImpact: No behaviour change for existing branch and remote names; the equivalence test guards it

errorCases.scenario: git_ls_remote cannot reach the remote
errorCases.detection: A non-zero exit classified by failureKind with network true (a network error text gives 'unreachable', a sign-in text 'missing-signin')
errorCases.response: A failure whose message carries git's stderr
errorCases.userImpact: branch-resolution.ts and handoff.ts keep their 'could not be reached' refusals, reading the reason from failure.message

errorCases.scenario: git_ls_remote returns no matching lines
errorCases.detection: Exit 0 with empty stdout
errorCases.response: Success with empty entries and symrefs
errorCases.userImpact: handoff.ts treats it as 'branch absent'; branch-resolution.ts as 'does not exist on remote'

errorCases.scenario: git_update_ref or git_rm times out or is killed
errorCases.detection: ShellResult.timedOut or code null with a kill signal
errorCases.response: A failure whose message says the outcome is unknown (mutating)
errorCases.userImpact: handoff.ts cleanup sees the failure and reports what it could not remove

errorCases.scenario: A gh_tracker owner, repo, org or login value is outside the name pattern (a '/', '?', '#', '%', whitespace, '.', '..' or a non-ASCII character), or a number is not a positive integer
errorCases.detection: The field's pattern (FieldSpec pattern carried into the flat input schema by fieldSchema) or integer minimum, which executeTool checks before it builds the approval request
errorCases.response: A rejected input failure produced by the executor; the approval gate is not called and no gh command runs
errorCases.userImpact: A bad name never reaches an approval prompt and cannot steer a tracker call to another endpoint

errorCases.scenario: Two ops of one family declare a shared field with different patterns
errorCases.detection: buildInputSchema compares the field's spec as JSON (the pattern is a string, so it is included) and finds a difference
errorCases.response: defineGhFamily throws 'field x is declared differently by two ops' when the module is loaded, so the build and the registration test fail
errorCases.userImpact: A family cannot ship with an op that is checked more loosely than its neighbour

errorCases.scenario: A gh_tracker value that passed its pattern or type (a since value, a label, a title) contains '&', '#', '/', spaces, '%' or non-ASCII where it enters a path or query
errorCases.detection: The path and qs variants pass every field value through encodeURIComponent; constants come only from the op definition
errorCases.response: The value is encoded inside its path segment or query value and can neither add a segment nor a query key; a list field joined by ',' encodes each member first
errorCases.userImpact: No input can steer a tracker call to another endpoint or add a query parameter

errorCases.scenario: An op declares a list-valued qs field without join, or a qs entry that is neither a constant nor a field entry
errorCases.detection: buildArgv's qs handling and the type of QsEntry; a family definition with such an entry fails the gh-op-table-qs test and throws when the argv is built in the family test
errorCases.response: The definition does not compile or the test fails; no argv is produced at run time from a malformed entry
errorCases.userImpact: A malformed query description is caught before release

errorCases.scenario: A paginated gh_tracker op (comments_list, issues_by_labels, issues_titles) reads a list that spans several pages
errorCases.detection: The argv carries --paginate and a fixed lit('-q', filter), so gh prints one JSON value per line across every page, and the op's builder reads the output with parseJsonLines; gh api --paginate on its own prints one JSON array per page, which a single JSON.parse cannot read
errorCases.response: Every page's items are returned in API order; the two issue listings exclude pull requests in the jq filter; an empty output is an empty list; blank lines are skipped
errorCases.userImpact: A list of more than 100 items returns every item, as the current wrappers do

errorCases.scenario: A paginated gh_tracker op prints a line that is not valid JSON
errorCases.detection: parseJsonLines returns { ok: false, line, text } for the first line that does not parse
errorCases.response: A rejected failure that names the 1-based line number and the first 200 characters of the line; no partial list is returned
errorCases.userImpact: The s10 caller maps it as it maps a failed command today

errorCases.scenario: gh project create (op project_create) prints JSON whose number is missing or not numeric, or prints text that is not JSON
errorCases.detection: The op's custom output builder parses stdout and checks that number is a number
errorCases.response: A rejected failure naming the unusable output; no { number, url } is returned
errorCases.userImpact: The s10 caller maps the failure to null exactly as ghCreateProject does today

errorCases.scenario: tools.call params are invalid: a missing field, a caller outside agent, daemon, workflow, a non-object input
errorCases.detection: The handler validates the params before building ToolDeps
errorCases.response: One 'error' frame { code: 'invalid-params', message } and the stream closes; no tool runs
errorCases.userImpact: The terminal client sees an invalid-params error

errorCases.scenario: tools.call names an unknown tool id
errorCases.detection: getTool returns undefined inside executeTool
errorCases.response: One 'done' frame whose result is a failed ToolResult of kind rejected; never an IPC error
errorCases.userImpact: The terminal client reports an unknown tool

errorCases.scenario: tools.call is handled without a trusted connection context
errorCases.detection: The handler finds context undefined when it builds ToolDeps
errorCases.response: sessionId is the plain string 'tools-call'; nothing else depends on it because git and gh tools keep no per-session state
errorCases.userImpact: None

errorCases.scenario: The client closes the tools.call stream while the call or its approval is pending
errorCases.detection: The server aborts the stream handler's signal when the socket closes
errorCases.response: A pending approval resolves 'cancelled'; a tool not yet started does not start; every running subprocess is killed with its process tree through the effective signal
errorCases.userImpact: The client that left sees nothing; the work is not done

errorCases.scenario: A destructive tool is called with valid input and no approval.subscribe client attached, or nobody answers in time
errorCases.detection: The approval gate returns 'no-client' or 'timed-out'
errorCases.response: failed('denied') with that denial; the tool does not run
errorCases.userImpact: The calling stage fails with the denial reported and does not continue (effective ac2)

errorCases.scenario: gh_tracker is defined but not registered
errorCases.detection: getTool returns undefined for gh_tracker in the registration test
errorCases.response: The registration test fails the build
errorCases.userImpact: A tool that exists in code but not in the registry is caught before release

errorCases.scenario: A tracker op returns data that does not match its declared output schema
errorCases.detection: The executor's output check after execute
errorCases.response: failed('schema-mismatch') built by the executor, with the raw output in failure.original cut to 4000 characters by the executor's own failed() helper
errorCases.userImpact: The caller gets a failure instead of unchecked data

errorCases.scenario: gh is not signed in or not installed when a tracker op runs
errorCases.detection: The shared gh failure helpers classify the error text and the spawn result
errorCases.response: missing-signin or missing-tool failure kinds, as the other gh tools do; the spawn-error branch keeps failure.original = stderr as today
errorCases.userImpact: The s10 tracker caller maps these to its own port failure

errorCases.scenario: A tracker op that creates an issue with a type is rejected because issue types are not enabled
errorCases.detection: The API answer is an HTTP 422 whose text names the issue type; the op sets the diagnostic field, so ghFailureOf puts the trimmed stderr (or stdout when stderr is empty) in failure.original
errorCases.response: A rejected failure with the API text in failure.original, cut by the seam itself to FAILURE_ORIGINAL_MAX_CHARS (4000) because the executor returns a tool's own failure unchanged; this is the text the s10 typed-issue fallback reads
errorCases.userImpact: No change to what the tracker creates today once s10 moves the caller

errorCases.scenario: A failing gh_tracker command writes more than 4000 characters of diagnostic text
errorCases.detection: ghFailureOf measures the trimmed text against FAILURE_ORIGINAL_MAX_CHARS
errorCases.response: failure.original holds the first 4000 characters; failure.message is unchanged
errorCases.userImpact: A large error body cannot flood the result

invariantsToPreserve.text: A tool whose declared output does not match, or that returns no data, fails with schema-mismatch and its result is not passed on (k2)

executeTool checks a tool's input schema before it builds the approval request, returns a failure a tool built itself unchanged, and only its own failed() helper caps failure.original at 4000 characters; buildApprovalRequest keeps the generic preview only when buildApprovalGate throws

A destructive call always asks whatever the caller, mode, setting or arguments say, and a denial is a failure value; the broker resolves 'cancelled' only for the signal it is given and otherwise waits for the 300000 ms approval timeout
Hooks run only after a successful, checked call, on the continuation after execute, and a hook failure never changes success into failure; they must not see any tool call's signal

git_push without a ref and git_reset build their approval preview by running git before any ask, outside any signal handling today; a killed read gives a failed read or undefined and a preview object, not an exception

Eight direct spawn sites in five tool files (exec-detached, k8s three, test, ssh two, aws logs) attach handlers to the child right after spawn, kill only the parent from an abort listener on deps.signal, run their own timers and settle on 'close' with no bound; each keeps its own progress frames and result text

A subprocess started through the shared helpers is cancellable today only where the tool forwards deps.signal (ghExec does; the legacy gh exports, the auth probe and git_diff do not); an AsyncLocalStorage context follows continuations, so clearing it takes an explicit run with an undefined store

registerTool overwrites an id with a warning; the git definitions are registered as withFailureNet spread copies, while the gh exports and defineGhFamily results are already the withGhFailureNet copies and are registered as they are; callTool's provenance check must pass for every registered tool of both families and refuse an unmarked replacement
Existing git tool ids, input shapes and approval classes keep their meaning (k7); the typing change is declaration-only and registration still wraps each definition with withFailureNet
git/index.ts is the only inventory of git definitions today and a list checked with satisfies verifies only its listed elements, so completeness needs the inventory test

FieldSpec carries no pattern and buildInputSchema rejects a field two ops declare differently (compared as JSON without description and values), so a pattern is a string and is compared; existing ops declare no pattern and keep their schemas

The tracker listing wrappers build 'state=all&per_page=100&labels=' + labels.map(encodeURIComponent).join(','), 'state=all&per_page=100' and 'per_page=100' with an optional since; the qs variant must reproduce these query strings exactly

The tracker listing wrappers read every page with 'gh api --paginate' plus a jq filter (-q) that prints one JSON value per line and then split the output into lines (src/workflow/tracker/github.ts lines 284, 351 and 362), because the pages of --paginate are separate JSON arrays and not one JSON document; the gh_tracker ops must return the same items in the same order
queryTasks returns hasNextPage (false when absent) and endCursor independently, and total only when issueCount is a number

ghCreateProject needs the JSON number and url of gh project create and returns null without a numeric number; ghFindProjectByTitle reads number, title, url and closed; the two boolean wrappers read only success

Failure objects of the existing gh tools do not change: for command-exit failures failure.original from ghFailureOf is set only from probe text unless an op opts in, and the spawn-error branch keeps original = stderr; existing ops use none of the new argument variants
Raw gh api stays excluded from the gh coverage table and the tracker family uses fixed endpoint templates only; no endpoint is an input
The refresh deadline stays 10 s (REFRESH_DEADLINE_MS) with one shared deadline started before the first git call, and the lock-lifetime reasoning beside it still holds

runShellBytes already tests an aborted signal before it starts and kills the process group; the lifecycle gains the same bounded settlement without changing results for a call that is neither aborted nor timed out

The callers of the four new git tools keep their semantics: identity.ts treats exit 1 with empty stdout as 'no email' and other failures as unavailable; handoff.ts treats empty ls-remote output as 'branch absent'; update-ref -d and rm --ignore-unmatch succeed when there is nothing to remove; ref and path acceptance equals isSafeRefName and assertSafeArg
The server aborts a stream handler's signal when the client closes the socket, TrustedRpcContext has no sessionId, and worker threads have no tool registry
tsc via tsconfig.json includes src/**/*.ts and does not check test files, so compile-time checks need their own config and the root config must exclude the fixtures

migration.backwardCompat: Every existing tool id, input shape and approval class is unchanged (k7), and no existing tool definition changes for cancellation except the five tool files that spawn their own processes, whose output, progress frames and result wording stay as recorded by the parity tests. A call without a signal and outside any context behaves as today; the ambient context is absent for code that does not run under executeTool (the indexer, the self-update, plain wrappers); a preview that runs no subprocess is built exactly as today; hooks behave as they do for a direct call whoever called the tool, because they run with no tool signal. The new ShellResult field, the readGit parameter, the OpDef diagnostic field, the FieldSpec pattern, the op-table argument variants, the parseJsonLines helper and the git_cat_file timeoutMs are optional or additive and no existing op uses the new variants or a pattern. A call that is neither aborted nor timed out settles as before; one that is killed now ends its whole process group and settles within 2 s, including for the five tool files (shell:exec-detached with a command form now ends its children too, which is the intended change); an already-aborted call spawns nothing. A tool run through executeTool with a signal now has its subprocesses killed when that signal aborts. callTool keeps its signature and works for every tool registered by registerGitTools (the wrapper marks its copy from the exported definition) and registerGhTools (the exported object is the registered object), and for a tool registered without a wrapper; only an unlinked replacement of a definition is refused. The existing git tools keep their ids and registration order; registration now iterates gitToolDefinitions. The new git tools accept every ref, remote and path their callers accept today. The tracker listing ops return the same items in the same order as the current wrappers. Existing gh failure objects, including the spawn-error branch, are unchanged because only the gh_tracker ops opt in, and the executor's treatment of failures is unchanged. The new tools and the new method are additive. The type check only adds a build step and the root build now excludes the fixtures. The scan runs in report mode, so the build does not fail on the sites s9 and s10 will move. The old wrappers and all call sites remain until s9 and s10.
